content_items.title: Introduction to the AI for Biodiversity Data session: what machine learning and LLMs actually do

programme.title: Introduction

actual.identification_notes: Chair (thanked as 'Martin', with 'Elena') introduces David Williamson to give the introduction session. The programmed 2-minute introduction had presenter TBC; Williamson's own talk 'AI Isn't Magic' (event-022) was cancelled after publication, and this ~9-minute introduction covers related ground (what ML/LLMs are, hallucination, measuring performance), so it is linked to the introduction slot rather than treated as the cancelled talk.

content_items.summary: David Williamson opened the SYM30A session with a primer on AI for a biodiversity audience: machine learning as approximating an unknown function y = f(x) from many labelled examples, illustrated with his own herbarium-sheet phenology classifier (buds, flowers, fruits). He then described large language models as next-token predictors trained on large text corpora, argued that 'reasoning' models only re-prompt themselves, and used examples completing 'Hymenoptera is a...' to argue that hallucinations are indistinguishable from true statements in the text and that there is no objective way to score such outputs. He closed by previewing the session's talks on machine vision, audio and validation.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: LLMs are word predictors with no notion of truth, so their outputs, including hallucinations, cannot be objectively scored from the text alone.
content_items.why_it_matters: It frames the whole session with a sceptical, mechanistic understanding of AI, reminding biodiversity researchers that performance measurement and truthfulness are open problems when using LLMs.
key_points: Most talks in the session concern machine learning, specifically deep learning (neural networks, transformers, LLMs), a subfield of AI going back to the 1960s or earlier.
Machine learning approximates an unknown function y = f(x) by training on many annotated examples, e.g. detecting buds, flowers and fruits on herbarium sheets.
LLMs predict the next token given a system prompt, user prompt and conversation context; tool calls and 'reasoning' are bolt-ons or self-prompting.
LLM performance is intuitively easy to judge but hard to measure objectively; they need huge training data and are expensive.
Hallucinations are plausible sentences that may or may not be true; there is no way to tell from the text itself.
themes_raw: large language models as next-token predictors
questions: How should one objectively score or rank different LLM outputs that are all plausible sentences?

notable_claims.claim: LLMs simply predict the next word based on the context window; there is no actual reasoning in the human sense.
There is no objective way to rank LLM completions or to tell a hallucination from a true fact based on the text alone.

examples_case_studies: Herbarium sheet phenology classifier predicting buds, flowers and fruits
Completions of 'Hymenoptera is a...' from different LLMs, including a Nordic-cuisine framing

representative_excerpt.text: But as you've seen, it's just a word predictor. It doesn't know what's true. It doesn't reason. It doesn't think.

notable_moments.description: Machine learning framed as solving y = f(x) with unknown f.
How LLMs predict the next word, with the 'grandmother exploded' example.

content_items.title: Delivering AI for biodiversity data in the public sector: data handling, security and humans-in-the-loop when small teams build at pace

programme.title: Delivering AI for biodiversity data in the public sector: data handling, security and humans-in-the-loop when small teams build at pace
programme.abstract: AI is reshaping how biodiversity data is collected, prepared and interpreted. It is also reshaping how the tools that do this work get built: practices loosely described as “vibe coding” or AI-assisted programming have changed what small teams can deliver, and how quickly. For public-sector bodies such as natural history museums, the opportunity is significant but the constraints are distinctive. Data governance, security baselines, accountability to research users, and the long-term stewardship of biodiversity records all shape what is possible. This talk offers a practitioner's perspective from the Natural History Museum, London, on applying AI in the development of biodiversity platforms in a public-sector context. It draws on experience building the AWS Data Ecosystem, the Museum's cloud-based platform for UK biodiversity data. The platform ingests biodiversity records gathered over time and streamed continuously from a range of sources, and serves research scientists as its primary user community. Two areas will be in focus. The first is data handling and security, including the questions raised when sensitive or pre-publication biodiversity data meets AI services in a public-sector environment. The second is human-in-the-loop design, and how to structure workflows so research scientists retain scientific authority over AI-assisted outputs while still benefiting from the productivity AI offers. The talk will also consider the financial and computational costs of AI-enabled approaches, particularly where cloud-based services are used operationally rather than experimentally. The talk is practice-oriented. It aims to share what is working, what is not, and where shared guidance from the TDWG community would help most.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Rachael Wiles'; she describes building the museum's Data Ecosystem product with AWS. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Rachel Wiles, product manager for the Natural History Museum's Data Ecosystem (a biodiversity data platform for largely urban UK nature built with AWS), described how a very small tech team uses AI tools to build at pace. She set out three boundaries of AI use: Claude Design for UI prototyping with dummy data, AWS Kiro as a code assistant running within the museum's AWS account for governance and logging, and GitLab agents for automated code review before deployment. She listed team rules (no AI acting on production data, no promoting unrewritten prototype code beyond dev, never bending the data model to a mock-up) and described human-in-the-loop verification tools (duplicate detection, PII/human detection, species clustering) surfaced as suggestions to expert verifiers. She asked the community for ideas on validation and provenance.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Small public-sector teams can use AI tools productively if they set clear boundaries between prototype, dev, test and production and keep expert humans in the loop.
content_items.why_it_matters: Offers a candid, practical model of AI governance for under-resourced biodiversity data teams, and raises the open problem of preserving provenance and credit when AI assists data workflows.
key_points: The Data Ecosystem aggregates eDNA, environmental sensing, community science and camera trap data with quality checks; 10 million records in its first six months.
Built in a four-year AWS partnership by a tiny team (a data engineer, a senior engineer and a product manager) with consultants filling gaps.
Claude Design is used for wireframes and prototypes with generated dummy data, avoiding museum IP or real records.
AWS Kiro sits inside the AWS account, allowing central access control and logging of model use.
GitLab agents add automated code review before deployment.
Organisations without an AI policy should get one now; retrofitting code to a policy is hard.
AI-assisted outputs (duplicate detection, PII checks, species clustering) arrive as suggestions for Centre for UK Nature experts to action.
themes_raw: AI governance in the public sector
questions: How can validation and provenance be maintained so original recorders get credit when AI is involved?
Could the public sector develop a shared position on AI services?

notable_claims.claim: The Data Ecosystem platform received 10 million records in its first six months live.
If your organisation doesn't have an AI policy, now is the time to get one.
AI is not going to outperform the expert verifiers in the Centre for UK Nature; it should make their workflow easier.

recommendations: Get involved in creating an organisational AI policy early rather than retrofitting.
Only allow AI-generated prototype code directly into dev when dev/test/prod boundaries exist.
Do not let AI tools change the data model to fit a mock-up.
future_work: Seeking community guidance on validation, provenance and a shared public-sector AI position.
examples_case_studies: NHM Data Ecosystem verification interface mock-up

q_and_a.answer_summary: Claude (Claude Design for wireframes, then Claude Code); different models have different styles, e.g. Opus is chatty and Fable more direct; Claude models are also accessible through Kiro.

content_items.title: Scalable Edge AI for Real-Time Biodiversity Monitoring: tracking invasive plant species in roadside imagery

programme.title: Scalable Edge AI for Real-Time Biodiversity Monitoring: A Case Study on Tracking Invasive Species in Roadside Imagery
programme.abstract:
Automated biodiversity monitoring is essential for tracking changes in species distributions and abundance, yet deploying cutting-edge AI on high-resolution imagery to detect diverse taxa remains challenging. While classical object detection models (e.g., YOLO) require exhaustive localized annotations that are infeasible to scale across massive taxonomies encompassing hundreds of thousands of plant species, global multi-label models offer a powerful alternative for complex species identification in a single forward pass.

In this work, we present a case study on continuous roadside monitoring to track invasive plants in near real-time. To capture localized invasions, vehicle-mounted cameras operate at high frequencies to guarantee dense spatial sampling. To develop an edge-deployable pipeline, we initially employed a multi-scale tiling framework with a Pl@ntNet model trained on global flora to automatically annotate complex roadside scenes. Through a process called knowledge distillation, these annotations are used to transfer the recognition capabilities of the heavy tiling framework (acting as a 'teacher') into a series of compact, fast models (the 'students'). These edge-deployed student models achieve performance comparable to the computationally demanding baseline across several datasets from different European countries.

We evaluate these student models on both species identification metrics and computational costs, highlighting critical operational trade-offs between image resolution, model parameters, and real-time latency. Ultimately, this framework paves the way for scalable, cost-effective ecological monitoring adaptable to diverse high-throughput data sources, including UAV surveys, plot imagery, and other extensive field campaigns.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as Giulio Martellucci from Montpellier; content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Giulio Martellucci presented work from a Biodiversa+ project in which vehicle-mounted cameras captured high-resolution roadside imagery across several countries (about 2,200 km of roads, 60 target alien plant species). Applying the Pl@ntNet classifier with multi-scale tiling works but takes around 10 seconds per image, so the team used knowledge distillation from the tiling 'teacher' to a global multi-label model: first the DINOv2 vision transformer, then a ConvNeXt (DINOv3-pretrained) model that scales linearly with resolution. The ConvNeXt model was both far cheaper (about 12 hours and 2.6 kWh versus 18 days and 138 kWh for the monitored roads) and more accurate on an expert-annotated test set.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Distilling a tiling-based plant identifier into a single ConvNeXt model makes high-resolution roadside invasive-species monitoring fast, cheap and more accurate.
content_items.why_it_matters: Transport corridors spread invasive plants; efficient models that could run in real time and be released open source make continental-scale early detection feasible.
key_points: Invasive plants are among the top five drivers of biodiversity loss; roads and railways accelerate seed dispersal.
Multi-scale tiling with the Pl@ntNet API (~70,000 species) gives presence/absence but is slow and costly.
Knowledge distillation trains a student to mimic the tiling teacher's predictions on whole high-resolution images.
Vision transformers scale quadratically with resolution; ConvNeXt scales linearly.
ConvNeXt processes about 14 images per second and uses dramatically fewer GFLOPs than tiling.
ConvNeXt achieved the best mAP and ROC metrics on a test set of 36 monitored species annotated by experts; tiling ranks true occurrences but produces too many false alarms.
Grad-CAM and dense-feature analyses show the model localises species even with occlusion and overlap.
datasets: Roadside high-resolution imagery (~2,200 km, 60 alien species)

notable_claims.claim: Covering all monitored roads with multi-scale tiling would take about 18 days and 138 kWh, versus about 12 hours and 2.6 kWh with the distilled ConvNeXt model.
The ConvNeXt model achieved the best results on the expert-annotated test set for both mean average precision and ROC-based metrics.

results_findings: ConvNeXt analyses about 14 images per second versus several seconds per image for tiling.
Tiling ranks true occurrences correctly but produces too many false alarms.
limitations: Performance depends on the number of expert-annotated images and plant size; better for trees than medium-sized species.
future_work: Release the model as open source.
Extend training to drone, citizen-science and plot imagery.
Extend monitoring to railway corridors.
Continue development in the Beagle European project.
examples_case_studies: Vehicle-mounted camera survey of roadsides across several European countries

q_and_a.question: Have you considered monitoring rivers, which are also invasion corridors?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Yes, rivers would be very interesting; longer term they would like to evaluate models on all plants in images, not just invasives.

q_and_a.question: How well did the model work depending on the growth stage of the plant?
q_and_a.answer_summary: Results depend on the number of expert-annotated images and on plant size; works better for trees than for medium species that are hard to capture.

notable_moments.description: Why tiling is too costly: ~10 s per image and ~70 days non-stop for all roads.

content_items.title: AI-vision for integrated management of pest insects and their natural enemies

programme.title: AI-vision for integrated management of pest insects and their natural enemies
programme.abstract: Precision farming is being adopted by many farmers, but the number of reliable tools for controlling weed, pest invertebrates and disease in arable cropping system is still quite limited. Most decision support models for plant protection against invertebrate pests consider the pest invertebrate, the plant and abiotic factors affecting them. Natural enemies of invertebrate pests are seldom considered as a factor in the decision support models. Recent advancements in precision technologies used in weed management rely on machine vision models and algorithms where weeds are identified from the cultivated plant and the chemical herbicides are applied only where weeds are identified, without broadcast uniform spraying an entire field, resulting in a 40-97% reduction in the use of chemical herbicides. Our focus in this project is therefore to reveal whether similar techniques could be adapted for precise control of pest insects while protecting and conserving their natural enemies. Our aim is to develop an Artificial Intelligence (AI) workflow that utilizes identification of pest insects and their natural enemies identification for automatic crop management systems. This work begins with the creation of a labelled and annotated image dataset for selected crops with the key pests and natural enemies. Thereafter, the dataset will be used to identify the best modelling toolbox for AI-based machine vision model for automatic species identification of pests and their natural enemies. The result will serve as basis toward designing a framework for pest monitoring and conservation biological control in the selected crops at field level.

actual.identification_notes: ASR renders the name as 'Reiter Ngimapi'; speaker says he is from NIBIO. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Ritter Guimapi of NIBIO presented an idea and work in progress: extending precision sprayer robots, which in Norway have cut herbicide use by 40-90% by dropping herbicide only on detected weeds, to insect pests within conservation biological control. The vision is a robot that distinguishes pests from beneficial natural enemies (e.g. parasitoids) and applies insecticide only to pests. He described why collecting representative training images has proven much harder than for weeds: pest-enemy interactions are transient and hard to time, insects are mobile, damaging life stages sit on leaf undersides, affordable equipment is needed, and regulations restrict releasing natural enemies in controlled settings. He invited suggestions on equipment and approaches.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Moving precision spraying from static weeds to mobile pests and their natural enemies is blocked mainly by the difficulty of collecting representative image data.
content_items.why_it_matters: Integrating AI vision into conservation biological control could reduce pesticide use while protecting beneficial insects, but data acquisition is the bottleneck.
key_points: Integrated Pest Management and conservation biological control aim to keep pests below thresholds while supporting beneficial organisms.
Precision sprayer robots in Norway reduce herbicide use by 40-90%, helped by regulations banning drone spraying.
Transfer learning was the first idea, but field data collection failed.
Challenges: timing of interactions, insect mobility, eggs and larvae on leaf undersides, cost of equipment, and national regulations.
A controlled environment is being explored but is not simple either.

notable_claims.claim: Precision sprayer robots have reduced herbicide use in Norway by between 40% and 90%.

limitations: Field image collection was unsuccessful; existing trolley-mounted top-view cameras designed for weeds are poorly adapted to insects.

q_and_a.answer_summary: One camera; the partners' trolley takes top-view pictures at fixed frequency, which worked for weeds but not for insects, so alternatives are being considered.

content_items.title: Soundscape China: Listening to the Sounds of Nature with AI

programme.title: Soundscape China - Listening to the Sounds of Nature with AI
programme.abstract:
With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and acoustic sensing technologies, the use of sound for biodiversity monitoring has evolved from localized experiments to widespread application. The construction of a national intelligent monitoring network based on natural sounds has become a key research direction in the field of ecological monitoring. The "Soundscape China" project is precisely centered on the goal of intelligent natural soundscape monitoring. It addresses multiple critical components-ranging from sensor development and intelligent species identification modeling to the construction of big data platforms-and is dedicated to creating an integrated technological chain that encompasses "acquisition, recognition, and management." The project strives to provide a standardized, replicable, and scalable model for the industry.

To date, Phase I of the "Soundscape China" project has deployed over 120 acoustic monitoring devices nationwide, which have automatically collected and aggregated more than 2 million valid recordings. The monitoring coverage spans diverse ecosystem types, including forests, wetlands, farmlands, grasslands, and deserts, thereby providing robust data support for national biodiversity monitoring. The project has been officially selected for inclusion in the United Nations' "Decade of Science" program. In the future, it aims to further expand the intelligent natural soundscape monitoring network, while also deepening cross-disciplinary practices such as citizen science education and sound art. This will promote multi-disciplinary synergy and foster an innovative framework of positive interaction among technology, ecology, and society.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Cong Lin' from the Chinese Academy of Sciences; the speaker asks to be called Colin. The ASR renders the institute as 'Institute of Geology' (likely Institute of Zoology). Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Congtian Lin presented Soundscape China, a national initiative to build a passive acoustic monitoring network, a nature-sound database and AI models, while involving citizen scientists and sound artists. The project tests sound sensors from different companies against standards (4G/5G data transfer, solar power, over 50 days' storage); about 280 devices have been deployed by over 110 participating organisations at more than 260 sites, yielding over 3.6 million records in one year. The platform includes a citizen-science recording app, an annotation tool with volunteers, a localised extension of Audubon Core, and a self-supervised pre-trained spectrogram model for sound event detection and classification, illustrated with bird-call activity patterns at three sites in Shandong Province.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Soundscape China is building a nationwide acoustic sensor network, database and AI models, gathering 3.6 million recordings in its first year.
content_items.why_it_matters: Standardised, large-scale acoustic data and open datasets are prerequisites for training reliable sound-recognition models and for using soundscapes as biodiversity indicators.

Framework: platform of sensors, models and database; services for data sharing, annotation, analysis and model training; audiences in monitoring, sound art and citizen science.

content_items.title: Cross-Modal Coordination for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale: Lessons from SmartWilds

programme.title: Cross-Modal Coordination for Biodiversity Monitoring at Scale: Lessons from SmartWilds
programme.abstract:
No single sensing modality is sufficient to monitor biodiversity at scale. Camera traps miss vocalizing birds, acoustic recorders miss silent species, drones struggle with species ID from altitude, and citizen science is opportunistic. Each modality has its own mature AI ecosystem (BirdNET, BioCLIP, MegaDetector, foundation models for drone imagery, iNaturalist), but automating biodiversity data collection, preparation, and interpretation at scale requires moving beyond single-modality pipelines toward cross-modal coordination, with smart sensors making decisions at the edge.

Coordinating across modalities is fundamentally a multi-scalar problem across both time and space. Standardizing these streams into datasets that support multimodal AI requires AI itself: foundation models for cross-modal alignment, LLM-assisted metadata extraction, and shared schemas like Darwin Core that make the result machine-actionable. We present SmartWilds, a co-located multimodal deployment at The Wilds Conservation Center, Ohio, combining camera traps, autonomous recording units, drones, citizen science, and field text across 220 hectares, with 380K Darwin Core occurrences and complete sensor configuration metadata.

We evaluate where each modality-specific AI pipeline is mature and where it is not, with drone species ID from altitude showing the largest gap, bird vocalization classification being robust but limited to vocal taxa, and camera-trap individual re-identification at scale remaining unsolved. We report annotation effort, computational cost, and known failure modes alongside performance, supporting honest assessment of which components are ready for edge deployment and which require centralized compute or human review.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded virtual presentation (programme marks it virtual). ASR renders the name as 'Jenna Klein'. The video restarted briefly at 01:22:22 after it ended; no live Q&A was possible, questions were directed to Whova, and a Whova poll was announced at 01:41:19.

content_items.summary: Jenna Kline, a postdoc at MIT, presented her PhD work reframing ecological sensing as an adaptive edge-systems problem in which AI closes the sensing loop. She first described autonomous drone systems for tracking herds that redefine the target as the herd, add behaviour-adaptive flight to reduce disturbance, and adapt paths to capture views needed for individual identification (tested in Ohio and Kenya). She then argued for cross-modal coordination among drones, camera traps, acoustic monitors, citizen science and GPS, presenting the SmartWilds dataset from a summer-long campaign at The Wilds safari park in Ohio: nearly 400,000 occurrences across five modalities with metadata enabling temporal and spatial cross-referencing against a known census. Synchronised traces from such datasets can inform provisioning decisions (models, hardware, sensor configuration, thresholds) before expensive field trials.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Coordinating multiple sensor modalities with AI at the far edge, informed by synchronised multimodal datasets like SmartWilds, can scale and adapt biodiversity monitoring.
content_items.why_it_matters: Moves monitoring from collect-then-analyse pipelines toward real-time adaptive sensing, and shows how multimodal benchmark datasets can de-risk the design of field systems.
key_points: Traditional workflows separate sensing, inference and analysis, preventing real-time adjustment and delaying insights.
'Far edge' means both remote field sites and constrained commodity hardware with latency and connectivity limits.
Autonomous drone work: herd tracking, behaviour-adaptive flight, and surface-of-interest-aware paths (e.g. elephant ears, zebra/giraffe flanks for individual ID).
AI in the loop increased the yield of usable data in field tests in Ohio and Kenya.
SmartWilds: 200-acre pasture with known census of milu deer, takin and Przewalski's horses; ~400,000 occurrences across five modalities.
Cross-modal triggers: a camera trap alarm could launch a drone; an acoustic event could activate camera traps; a citizen science observation could trigger other sensors.
Biodiversity datasets must be usable by robotics and AI research communities.
methods: synchronised trace replay for system provisioning
questions: How much compute and energy are needed, is solar sufficient, and which sensors should be deployed?

notable_claims.claim: The SmartWilds field campaign produced almost 400,000 occurrences across five modalities.

representative_excerpt.text: So in summary, cross-modal coordination can assist in scaling data collection, enable real-time adaptivity, support non-invasive monitoring, and advance better-informed conservation policies.

content_items.title: Trapper 2.0: scalable, open-source platform for managing camera trapping projects with integrated AI pipelines

programme.title: Trapper 2.0: scalable, open-source platform for managing camera trapping projects with integrated AI pipelines
programme.abstract:
Camera trapping has become a powerful tool for wildlife monitoring, but the resulting multimedia datasets, often comprising millions of images and videos, present significant analytical challenges. Manual annotation is time-consuming, expensive, and difficult to scale, making AI integration essential for modern biodiversity monitoring workflows.

Trapper is an open-source, web-based platform designed to manage camera trap data at any scale, from individual research projects to large citizen science initiatives. It allows users to build automated AI analysis pipelines consisting of a variety of open-source AI models used for object detection, tracking objects in videos, species classification and distance and movement speed detection. Trapper’s architecture allows for easy integration of new models as they are being developed.

The results of AI analysis can be reviewed and corrected by human experts. This human-in-the-loop approach maximises annotation efficiency without sacrificing data quality. The recently released version, Trapper 2.0, features support for processing videos as well as images. Trapper is compatible with the Camtrap DP data standard, ensuring interoperability with GBIF and broader biodiversity data infrastructures.

An important feature of Trapper’s design is deployment flexibility. The entire Trapper stack, including the AI processing components, can be run on a personal computer, a local server or a cloud server, as well as on microservers like Raspberry Pi. AI processing can be done using CPU alone, with GPU acceleration or using Hailo-based processing, enabling computation on edge devices. This helps to significantly decrease computation costs, making AI-assisted biodiversity monitoring more accessible even with limited resources.

speakers.name: Karolina Kuczkowska
speakers.affiliation: GBIF Poland / Open Science Conservation Fund

actual.identification_notes: Speaker introduces herself as data manager at the Polish GBIF node working at the Open Science Conservation Fund (Białowieża). Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Karolina Kuczkowska presented Trapper, a ten-year-old open-source data infrastructure for camera trapping projects, and its forthcoming version 2, which adds video analysis. Its customisable AI pipeline chains object detection (MegaDetector or YOLO models), species classification, multi-object tracking with custom post-processing, pose estimation and, in development, depth estimation for population density methods, with experts correcting results in the interface. New models can be added via a form or a Python connector class. Trapper runs wherever Docker runs, from cloud servers to NVIDIA Jetson or Raspberry Pi; the WildLabs-funded Trapper Keeper field box enables edge processing, which she argued is key for hotspots without infrastructure, data security and lower environmental impact. Data export in Camtrap DP allows publication to GBIF via the IPT, with direct publication planned.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Trapper 2.0 offers an open, model-agnostic, edge-deployable pipeline for camera trap photos and videos with expert review and Camtrap DP export.

content_items.title: Are plant image datasets ready for AI-enabled community assessment? A systematic review of bias, representativeness and annotation quality

programme.title: Assessing the Readiness of Plant Image Datasets for AI-enabled Spatially Explicit Ecological Monitoring: A Systematic Review of Bias, Representativeness, and Annotation Quality
programme.abstract:
Despite rapid advances in AI models, the applicability of ecological monitoring remains constrained by limitations in dataset quantity and quality. While most plant image datasets focus on classification for species identification, object detection and segmentation datasets remain underdeveloped. These tasks are critical for spatially explicit ecological inference, including individual localisation, abundance estimation, and vegetation structure analysis.

This review systematically identified and analysed plant image datasets developed for ecological monitoring. An assessment framework inspired by clinical image datasets evaluation was adapted to ecological monitoring requirements and applied to 42 datasets. The framework evaluated dataset scale, ecological representativeness, annotation protocols, and data management practices.

The results revealed that most datasets lacked clearly documented annotation protocols and cross-annotator consistency controls, undermining the reliability of annotations as ground truth for AI-based ecological inference. Inconsistencies in taxonomic and geographic distribution further limit both model generalisability and the applicability of image-based monitoring at global scales. Agricultural weed detection dominated current applications, while broader biodiversity monitoring remained limited.

These findings highlight that while datasets are increasingly available, their design is often not aligned with the ecological levels required for biodiversity monitoring. Both annotation quality and ecological representativeness of available datasets fall short of the requirements for robust and generalisable image-based monitoring. Future work should prioritise ecologically representative and well-documented datasets for biodiversity monitoring.

content_items.summary: Yuchen Zhao (Newcastle University) argued that ecological AI is constrained less by model architecture than by the quantity and quality of training data. She presented a four-dimension framework, inspired by clinical reporting frameworks and FAIR, for assessing plant image dataset readiness: training-relevant characteristics, image acquisition characteristics, annotation protocol, and accessibility. A systematic review of in-situ, non-crop plant object detection and segmentation datasets screened 360 unique studies and found only 40 eligible datasets, with strong geographic bias toward Europe and Asia, a dominance of agricultural applications (19 of 40 focused on wheat), neglect of background plants, and generally unsatisfactory annotation protocols.

content_items.title: The WildLIVE Portal: Towards Scalable Wildlife Monitoring through the Integration of Citizen Science and Human-in-the-Loop AI Workflows

programme.title: The WildLIVE Portal: Towards Scalable Wildlife Monitoring through the Integration of Citizen Science and Human-in-the-Loop AI Workflows
programme.abstract: Global biodiversity monitoring delivers an ever-increasing volume of recorded data, with even medium-sized projects gathering data in the order of hundreds of thousands of images annually. These vast amounts of data frequently overwhelm the manual review capacity of domain experts and small research teams. As a result, the scale of these observations creates significant bottlenecks that hinder timely data annotation and analysis for conservation efforts. AI-generated baseline annotations can reduce this workload, but they still require expert review before they can be treated as reliable scientific evidence. The primary challenge lies in establishing trust and quantifiable confidence in these annotations, regardless of their source. To address this challenge, Senckenberg’s WildLIVE portal combines AI workflows with Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) refinement. The platform supports multi-model object detection, including open-vocabulary approaches in which detections can be guided by textual category descriptions rather than being limited to a fixed label set. Through an active-learning infrastructure, the platform prioritises observations most in need of review, directing citizen scientists and domain experts toward images where labelling effort can have the greatest impact on model confidence. These evaluations are preserved as layered annotations linking back to AI4WildLIVE’s FAIR Digital Object-based data model. By integration of an AI-assisted annotation pipeline, active learning, AI-readiness of data and citizen science engagement, the WildLIVE portal establishes a shared, human and machine operable collaborative framework through which biodiversity monitoring data becomes a trusted, community-wide scientific resource.

content_items.title: HerbAudit: Validating AI-Driven Herbarium Transcriptions

programme.title: HerbAudit: Validating AI-Driven Herbarium Transcriptions
programme.abstract: Millions of herbarium specimens are now digitized and accessible online, yet transforming specimen label images into structured, queryable data remains a major bottleneck in biodiversity informatics. While OCR and LLM technologies are increasingly applied to this challenge, the community lacks a shared framework to measure tool performance and identify data gaps. To fill this gap, we developed HerbAudit, an open source tool combining herbarium label transcription with systematic quality evaluation, to be publicly available by September 2026. We also compiled a gold standard benchmark dataset of 90 typed and handwritten specimens from 63 institutions worldwide, each manually transcribed using Label Studio. HerbAudit consists of two core components. The transcription component builds on VoucherVision logic, processing images via LLMs like Google Gemini and OpenAI to output Darwin Core formatted data. It includes a resolution adjustment submodule and reports estimated cost and carbon footprint metrics per image. The evaluation component offers two distinct pathways. First, OCR tool outputs are compared directly against the gold standard manual annotations. Second, AI tool predictions in Darwin Core format are cross checked against GBIF and POWO, incorporating a built-in synonym check. Fields are scored using domain specific methods, such as geographic coordinates via the Haversine formula and author names via Character Error Rate. Users can apply transcription and AI evaluation to their own datasets, with the latter requiring records on GBIF to pinpoint errors and visualize where tools fall short. All results are compiled into an interactive HTML report, giving developers and researchers a shared foundation to benchmark, compare, and improve digitization pipelines.

content_items.summary: Dilara Ağacık presented HerbAudit, a tool that both transcribes herbarium labels with a single multimodal AI call (after LeafMachine2 label detection) into Darwin Core, and evaluates transcriptions against manual annotations or GBIF records using field-specific scoring that avoids wrongly penalising AI: taxonomic synonym checks, order-independent collector matching, date-distance scoring, ISO country normalisation and transliteration, word-based locality matching and Haversine distance for coordinates. On a manually annotated benchmark of 90 specimens from 63 institutions, AI transcription averaged 94% accuracy; a Gemini 'Lite' model (ASR 'Gemini 3.5 Lite') offered the best accuracy-to-cost trade-off, the local Gemma model came close at zero API cost, and HerbAudit outperformed other tools with full extraction coverage. content_items.title: AI-assisted digitisation of printed identification keys: from book to structured data in minutes

programme.title: AI-assisted digitisation of printed identification keys: from book to structured data in minutes
programme.abstract:
Printed identification keys are a major reservoir of curated biodiversity knowledge, but mobilising them into machine-readable form is hampered by the cost of expert transcription, taking days of work per key. We present a working pipeline that produces structured-key drafts from heterogeneous sources in minutes.

The pipeline runs in two stages. An extraction agent (local OCR plus targeted vision reads of figures) builds a taxa tree and atomic characters. A fresh-context audit agent then re-reads the draft against the source, catching character states that overlap or leave source-mentioned values uncovered, numeric characters without actual measurements, and described traits missing from the output - fixing each until a deterministic verifier signs off. Two transformations bridge dichotomous prose and matrix-form output: splitting bundled traits ("brown hairs, green stem, white dots") into separate characters, and merging synonymous states ("whitish yellow" / "pale yellow") across the file. All such decisions are documented for the taxonomist to consider; target output is an editable draft, not a finished publication.

We have run the pipeline on various inputs: dichotomous keys in scanned books, combined prose descriptions of species from multiple field guides, and online interactive keys. We also include a domain-aware language translation step which maintains context and user-provided terminology.

Costs depend on the input format and structure, but are limited to at most a few dollars per species, and will be presented in detail. The Clavis output format and its place in combined AI-plus-key identification workflows are addressed in a companion talk in "May the Data Be Structured" (SYM32).

content_items.summary: Wouter Koch explained why identification keys remain essential alongside image recognition (pictures often lack diagnostic characters, models do not explain why, and training needs labelled data) and showed combining image-recognition top-5 suggestions with digital keys to ask only the discriminating questions. He then described an LLM agent pipeline, demonstrated on a new key to Norwegian rodents compiled from six books none of which alone covered all species: local OCR, one agent per source extracting modular, precise statements (using both keys, descriptions and images), a fresh audit agent with 'nothing to defend', merging and harmonising characters (with documented decisions and moving shared traits to higher taxa, optional translation), and a grounding agent verifying every statement against the sources. A single key costs about $10 in an hour, six books under about $30, producing a draft for expert review rather than a finished key; generated illustrations still fail.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: An agentic LLM pipeline can turn printed keys and descriptions into a structured draft identification key for tens of dollars, shifting experts from transcribers to reviewers.

content_items.title: AI-assisted georeferencing a posteriori of herbarium specimens: a case study on Italian herbaria

programme.title: AI-assisted georeferentiation a-posteriori of herbarium specimens: a case study on Italian herbaria
programme.abstract:
Italy’s largest herbaria have recently undergone a large-scale digitization, making more than 4 million specimens available online through the national portal PlantData and the GBIF. Most specimens only had textual locality descriptions without geographic coordinates, limiting their use in many ecological analyses such as species distribution models. To address this limitation, we started a process of georeferentiation a-posteriori.

The data presented different challenges: locality labels were often in Latin or partially illegible, mixing locality names with habitat notes, altitude and collector annotations. Initial georeferencing approaches using national gazetteers and OpenStreetMap Nominatim achieved success rates below 10%, as geocoding services were frequently confused by excessive contextual details in locality strings. Workflows based on Google Maps APIs improved results (~50%) but remained highly sensitive to spelling errors and historical orthographic variants.

Thus, we developed pipelines that combine lightweight large language models (LLMs) with geocoding services. The models use the full label context to separate locality names from ancillary text and correct spelling inconsistencies before georeferencing. Small LLMs combined with Nominatim achieved ~71% successful georeferentiations at very low cost. Small LLMs paired with Google Maps improved this result to ~78%, while using Frontier LLMs reached up to 84% accuracy, but they remain too expensive for high volume data.

This approach shows that AI can assist and accelerate the process of georeferencing a-posteriori herbarium specimens. Small LLMs can achieve strong performance and, along with Nominatim, can be fully self-hosted, reducing reliance on external APIs and services.

content_items.summary: Matteo Conti described a workflow for retrospective georeferencing of specimens from a national project digitising 12 large Italian herbaria (about four million specimens). Standard tools performed poorly on historical, often Latin, handwritten localities (Nominatim georeferenced under 10% and Google Maps about 50%). The six-step workflow uses an LLM parser, with dynamically injected few-shot examples matched by language and spatial relation, to extract toponyms, habitats, elevations and relations; matches toponyms against three gazetteers; ranks and filters candidates; uses an LLM judge to accept, flag for review or reject; and adjusts coordinates and uncertainty for relational localities. Run locally with Gemma it produced more than double Google Maps' correct georeferences with fewer wrong ones, and Gemma and Gemini Flash Lite flagged all coarser and wrong results for human review.

content_items.title: Towards Scalable Trait Measurements from Digitized Specimens

programme.title: Towards Scalable Trait Measurements from Digitized Specimens
programme.abstract:
The increasing digitization of natural history collections creates opportunities for large-scale extraction of quantitative specimen traits. Morphological traits such as specimen shape and size are important for research in ecology and biodiversity. To obtain reliable and comparable traits from images, pixel measurements are converted into metric units using a scale conversion factor (CF), typically calculated by measuring pixel distances between ruler tick marks.

We build upon our previous work on automated ruler detection and scale estimation for herbarium specimens by improving its robustness and scalability. The original approach relied solely on image keypoint matching for CF estimation, which performed well for conventional rulers but was unreliable for simpler ruler types. We extend the original method with a hierarchical framework that first identifies the ruler type and then selects the most appropriate method for CF estimation. These simple rulers, such as lines, blocks, and grids, are processed differently, using a combination of computer vision methods and LLMs.

To evaluate this new approach, our dataset has been expanded beyond herbaria to a broader range of domains, including zoological, entomological, geological, and microscopy images. Furthermore, we show how the estimated CF values can be stored as standardized metadata to support interoperability and how markers can simplify scale estimation in future digitization workflows. Finally, we show how the scale estimation method can be combined with segmentation models to automatically extract specimen traits.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Kenzo Melville'; content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Kenzo Milleville presented a method to convert pixel measurements on specimen images into metric units by reading the ruler on the sheet. Instead of predicting scale directly, the ruler is detected and normalised, similar rulers are retrieved from an annotated reference set with a CLIP-like similarity model, and a keypoint-matching model transforms the known tick marks onto the new image, requiring in principle only one labelled example per ruler type. The reference set grew to about 2,000 rulers (21,000 annotated points, ~350 institutions), and 96% of predictions now have under 1% error (mean ~0.3%, below the ~0.8% manual annotation error). A proof of concept with Segment Anything 3 measured leaf sizes across taxa and geography. He recommended including ArUco markers or QR codes of known size during digitisation, and noted a proposal to Audiovisual Core to standardise such metadata and the idea of sharing length annotations via DiSSCo.

content_items.title: Reconsidering the original vision for a global biodiversity information facility

programme.title: Reconsidering the original vision for a global biodiversity information facility
programme.session: SYM08A BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
programme.abstract: A global biodiversity information facility was recommended in 1999 by the OECD Biodiversity Informatics Subgroup of the Megascience Forum. In 2001, 25 years ago this month, GBIF, the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, embarked to meet the challenges outlined by the Forum. Soon thereafter the scope was narrowed due to limited funding to meet the challenge. The original vision was a more encompassing of data from literature, traits, and taxonomy. GBIF focused on species occurrences and community building. Critically GBIF continues to grow as an intergovernmental organization, not affiliated with the United Nations, which provides sustainability. Other important infrastructure projects such as BHL, COL, EOL (and others) filled the void but lacked GBIF’s governance framework. What if the original vision had been funded and pursued? Would it have worked? Given the considerable stress on science and infrastructures today, could the original vision work now?

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by Nicole Kearney as GBIF Executive Secretary. A long Q&A/discussion followed, which is kept with this talk.

content_items.summary: Joe Miller, GBIF Executive Secretary, offered a 'provocation' for GBIF's 25th anniversary: a personal timeline of biodiversity infrastructures (LTER, GenBank, TDWG, the 1992 Rio conventions, TreeBASE, Species 2000/Catalogue of Life, OBIS, GEO BON, BHL, EOL) leading to the 1999 OECD Megascience Forum recommendation for a Global Biodiversity Information Facility. He revisited the report's figure: GBIF was to encompass names, specimen data, a 'species bank' and biodiversity literature, but funders narrowed it to occurrence data and the nodes network, and other initiatives (Catalogue of Life, BHL, EOL) filled the gaps. Today's landscape achieves 'synergisms among existing investments' through collaboration, but he asked whether that is enough. The Q&A debated how to make the case for closer BHL-GBIF links: Miller said the community, not the Secretariat, must bring such a case to the Governing Board; Donat Agosti argued literature data are already integrated at scale; and a commenter called for a new, AI-informed, impact-focused community vision.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: GBIF achieved its 1999 vision only partially and through a network of collaborating infrastructures; the community must decide whether that is enough and articulate the next vision.
content_items.why_it_matters: It reframes the relationship between GBIF, BHL and related infrastructures as an unfinished design question, relevant to their sustainability and future integration.
key_points: The 1999 OECD report proposed a distributed system of interlinked, interoperable databases and tools.
Original content areas: catalogue of names, specimen data, species bank, biodiversity literature, linked to sequence, geospatial, climate and ecological data.
Limited funding narrowed GBIF's scope to occurrence data and the nodes network.
GBIF now has 70 member nations and around 300 businesses sharing data.
Catalogue of Life collaboration ended duplication and benefits both organisations.

Donat Agosti: 62,000 GBIF datasets derive from literature; new Pensoft/EJT publications reach GBIF within 24 hours with material citations linked to text positions.

questions: Is the current collaborative network 'enough' relative to GBIF's original vision?
What is the compelling case for closer BHL-GBIF integration, and who should make it?

notable_claims.claim: Funders scaled back GBIF's breadth to species occurrence data and the nodes network; there was insufficient funding for taxonomy, the species bank and literature.
GBIF has 70 member nations in its governance.
It is not up to the Secretariat to decide; the community needs to go to the Governing Board saying 'we think we need this'.
62,000 datasets in GBIF are from literature, and new Pensoft/EJT publications are in GBIF within 24 hours.

recommendations: The community should develop a consensus 21st-century vision drawing on new technology (AI) and demonstrated impact.
examples_case_studies: 1999 OECD Megascience Forum figure of GBIF's original content areas
GBIF-Catalogue of Life collaboration

q_and_a.question: How would you sell a closer BHL-GBIF link to the GBIF Governing Board?
q_and_a.answer_summary: The community, not the Secretariat, should make that case to the Governing Board, as happened with Catalogue of Life; Kearney responded that literature is the source of truth for names and linking species pages to literature is BHL's aim.

q_and_a.question: Aren't literature data already integrated at scale (62,000 datasets, 24-hour flow)?

content_items.title: For the Birds: Adapting Archives and Extracting Data for the Biodiversity Heritage Library

programme.title: For the Birds: Adapting Archives and Extracting Data for the Biodiversity Heritage Library
programme.session: SYM08A BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
programme.abstract: In December 2025, University of South Florida Libraries’ was honored to join the Biodiversity Heritage Libraries as a member, as well as to provide redundancy support for the technical team. As part of this new step, the team at USF is curating materials from their more than 30 collections of Florida Environment and Natural History (FLENH) materials and their extensive rare books collections. Ornithological research, including published and unpublished works, form the core of these holdings. While mixed in their formatting, the materials are rich in data that remained layered behind human prose, handwritten notes, and inconsistent checklists. Making these materials computer readable and adaptable for scientists to process at scale requires a heavy human lift. From local Audubon Society sanctuary records to the vast holdings of the Searchable Ornithological Research Archive (SORA), USF is exploring existing and adapted methods for ingesting their content into BHL over the next few years. Along the way, the team is working with scientists and student interns in various fields to test the accuracy of human and AI-methods to extract data. The team is hopeful that its efforts will provide a fresh case study for loading archival materials that can build on the work of other BHL members while leveraging internal expertise in cataloging, copyright, digital preservation, GIS, and data management. This talk will showcase the possibilities and priorities for the more than 106,000 already digitized records across the FLENH collections.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced by Kearney as 'Amanda Bozarth' and Sydney Jordan; Amanda presents first, then Sydney from 06:11:29. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Amanda Boczar and Sydney Jordan described the University of South Florida Libraries' environmental archives and its new BHL partnership. Anecdotes illustrated the stakes: digitised ornithological records helped establish the American flamingo as native to Florida, while nearly 100 years of Egmont Key records were likely destroyed by Hurricane Milton. After being turned away while BHL was closed to new members, USF joined the consortium in December and has spun up a redundant instance of the Macaw ingest platform on its AWS cloud, with public launch planned for mid-October. Sydney described the FLENH collections (38 archival collections, SORA's 87,000 articles, 112,000 records and 6.7 million downloads), rights and accessibility (WCAG 2.1) obligations, and early tests showing AI extraction of handwritten tabular field data introduces significant errors requiring human correction.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: USF is strengthening BHL's infrastructure via a redundant Macaw ingest instance while working to bring vulnerable Florida environmental archives and their data into BHL.
content_items.why_it_matters: Shows how a partner institution can underpin a transitioning infrastructure, and highlights both the value and the difficulty of extracting data from handwritten archival field records.
key_points: USF holdings are mainly historical ornithological and marine science records collected on paper.
Florida's climate, storms and unstable funding threaten archives stored in attics, storage units and marina lockers.
Macaw redundancy adds a third ingest route alongside Smithsonian and BHL Australia; first onboarding planned for November.
USF adopted the Searchable Ornithological Research Archive (SORA) when its host could no longer sustain it.
108 items (~2,800 pages) uploaded during early testing.
Field notes and warden reports mix qualitative and quantitative data in non-standard formats and often prose.
Aggregated published datasets often omit variables like temperature and tides found in raw field notes.

notable_claims.claim: USF's Macaw instance has been fully spun up, with public launch to consortium members planned for mid-October and first onboarding in November.
The digitised environmental collection has more than 112,000 records and close to 6.7 million downloads, 4.4 million from SORA.
Early AI extraction of handwritten tabular data showed significant errors, sometimes reducing a count from triple to single digits.

limitations: Rights clearance and redaction are complex; only a small fraction of holdings is online.
future_work: Ingest archival material at scale building on BHL Field Notes workflows or OAI-PMH.
Help draft metadata documentation via BHL's Metadata and Cataloging committee.
Append transformed datasets when ingesting material.

Egmont Key records lost to Hurricane Milton
Oral history with an environmental journalist on Tampa Bay

content_items.title: BHL and the Planetary Knowledge Base: Structuring Biodiversity Literature for the Next Generation

programme.title: BHL and the Planetary Knowledge Base: Structuring Biodiversity Literature for the Next Generation
programme.session: SYM08A BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
programme.abstract:
As BHL enters its second decade, the Natural History Museum (NHM) is assisting in its evolution into a machine-actionable, FAIR-aligned biodiversity information infrastructure. This work is connected to NHM's Planetary Knowledge Base (PKB), which integrates fragmented natural history literature, collections, observations, genetic and environmental data into an explainable system for research, policy and action for nature.

The BHL work focuses on developing a biodiversity knowledge-extraction and discovery layer that operates alongside the BHL, linking users back to BHL pages, publications and metadata while enabling new forms of structured search and analysis. NHM has prototyped workflows that transform BHL's page-centric volumes into structured, machine-actionable scholarly resources through modern OCR, article-level segmentation, figure and table extraction, persistent identifier assignment, and entity extraction for taxa, people, institutions, localities, specimen identifiers, habitats and stratigraphy.

These outputs will support semantic discovery, programmatic reuse, knowledge graph construction, and alignment with biodiversity infrastructures such as GBIF, Catalogue of Life, Wikidata, GRSciColl, etc. All extracted entities and relationships retain provenance links to the original BHL pages and bibliographic records, with confidence and workflow metadata. The dataset also serves as a foundational evidentiary layer for the Planetary Knowledge Base (PKB), helping ground biodiversity knowledge in the underlying BHL literature.

These activities position BHL as a distributed, resilient, interoperable evidentiary layer for biodiversity research, connected to specimens, taxa, collections, observations, and external datasets.

actual.identification_notes: ASR renders the speaker as 'Hiru Sku' and later 'Harris Goo'/'Kee Harris'; she says she is from the NHM London. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Qianqian Hiris Gu described NHM London's work making BHL machine-readable and connecting it to the NHM's Planetary Knowledge Base. Building on Neil Brummitt's decade of trait extraction from English-language BHL literature (about 700,000 trait terms across 81 standardised traits), an AWS prototyping sprint of four weeks on under 40,000 pages of a botanical journal combined modern OCR with computer vision for article title-page detection (~98%, ~100% with a table of contents), entity extraction (taxa, people, localities, institutions, habitats; F1 ~96%) into a knowledge graph and GraphRAG search. Benchmarking with BHL-provided ground truth showed printed text reaching human-level transcription, and word-level confidence from OCR models can gate what goes back into BHL. The work is now in production: re-OCR of the whole corpus by around January 2027, an open gold-standard dataset in early 2027, and an Explorer interface in Q2 2027.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: NHM is re-OCRing all of BHL with modern models and extracting entities into a knowledge graph, with confidence gating to protect BHL data quality.
content_items.why_it_matters: Turning BHL's 64 million pages into structured, linkable data could unlock huge amounts of trait, taxon and specimen information for research and infrastructure links.
key_points: Four pages of a 2002 publication contained 142 data points; BHL has about 64 million pages.
Previous trait extraction covered only English literature and 17% of accepted flowering plants.
Earlier pipelines needed a separate model per task; LLMs/VLMs allow more in one pass.
Article segmentation via title page detection enables assigning DOIs and references.
Word-level OCR confidence creates a barrier against ingesting hallucinated text into BHL.
Production also extracts specimen identifiers to link back to GBIF and stratigraphy data.

notable_claims.claim: Article title page detection achieved around 98%, and around 100% when a table of contents is available.
Entity extraction reached an F1 score of about 96%.
For printed text, modern OCR already achieves human accuracy in transcription.

results_findings: Neil Brummitt's work extracted ~700,000 trait terms across 81 standardised traits, covering >100,000 descriptions and 60,000 species.
limitations: Handwritten and raw ground truth show higher error rates.
Trait extraction so far only covers English literature.
future_work: Complete re-OCR of the whole BHL corpus by end of 2026 or January 2027.
Publish an open gold standard dataset in early 2027.
Launch the Explorer in Q2 2027.
Link extracted specimen identifiers to GBIF.
examples_case_studies: Four-week AWS prototype on a botanical journal (<40,000 pages)

content_items.title: Possibilities to enhance the semantic navigation of BHL: further developing the 'unit of work'

programme.title: Possibilities to enhance the semantic navigation of BHL - further developing the "unit of work"
programme.session: SYM08A BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Reimagining BHL: Foundations, Partnerships and Future Infrastructure
programme.abstract:
The BHL data resource includes page images, scanned OCR text and bibliographic metadata regarding its holdings. Data are ingested into BHL using the units of volumes, parts and pages. Later projects such as biostor have asserted more useful units of work such as articles within serial titles by allocating a series of pages to an article with a title and authorship. The BHL user interface has a long-standing feature enabling navigation via the results of taxonomic indexing, which looks for occurrences of scientific names within page texts.

This talk will discuss the possibilities for building on the article identification concept and creating more domain specific units of work from the examination of contents pages, standard body pages and index pages to determine the layout and organisation of the information held within the part. Units of work could comprise biographical entries organised alphabetically by person name, dictionary or glossary entries organised alphabetically, species entries in specimen catalogues, monographs and floristic works ordered taxonomically, or field work sites and gazetteer entries organised geographically. Identification of these would help drive wider use of BHL-mobilised data and build stronger links with user communities such as those working with biographical data about collectors and identifiers in the Bionomia project, those seeking historical geographic data for georeferencing and taxonomic projects such as the World Flora Online

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Nikki Nicholson' from Kew; content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Nicky Nicolson, starting from Kew's IPNI (funded by Darwin's legacy) which indexes names to the exact page, argued that BHL has been built primarily as a library (volumes, pages, then articles via BioStor), whereas as a biodiversity data source its pages are richly structured, containing people directories, multilingual glossaries and gazetteers that are not best reached via articles. She contrasted bottom-up entity discovery across 64 million pages with top-down, community-driven subsetting, and proposed that BHL learn from GBIF's hosted portals: branded, pre-filtered views that let communities and funders see their slice (e.g. DiSSCo UK), which could also address contributors like Madrid who keep content out of BHL's viewer for branding reasons. Comments from Donat Agosti (GBIF hosted portals for journals) and a TaxonPages developer (need for BHL API endpoints) followed.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Letting user communities carve BHL into branded, pre-filtered 'hosted portals' could serve diverse needs, satisfy funders and drive innovation.
content_items.why_it_matters: Rethinking BHL's units of navigation beyond volumes and articles could expose the structured entities in literature to the communities that need them.
key_points: IPNI indexes to the exact page and structured data, not just the article.
BHL was populated as a library: scanned volumes, OCR, then post-accession article identification.
Name indexing is to name strings, not the structured entities they represent.
Pages often function as printed databases: people, glossaries, gazetteers.
GBIF (25) vs BHL (20): GBIF used later years to stitch data together (e.g. clustering) and build hosted portals.
Funders want acknowledgement ('does it acknowledge my investment?') and users ask 'is it relevant for me?'.
questions: Should BHL entity discovery be bottom-up across all pages or top-down via specialist communities?

notable_claims.claim: BHL has largely been populated as a library, focusing on the library part rather than the biodiversity part.
Madrid contributes thousands of useful volumes that cannot be viewed in BHL itself because they want a branded interface.

recommendations: Let user communities define subsets of BHL through hosted-portal-style interfaces.
examples_case_studies: DiSSCo UK hosted portal on GBIF
Multilingual glossary and gazetteer pages in BHL

q_and_a.answer_summary: Acknowledged.

content_items.title: Biological occurrence data from historic scientific correspondence: enabling automated approaches for structured data extraction from body text

programme.title: Biological occurrence data from historic scientific correspondence: enabling automated approaches for structured data extraction from body text
programme.session: SYM08B BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
programme.abstract:
Historical species occurrence data are essential for incorporating the past into analyses of biodiversity change. In addition to sources specifically intended to document occurrences, such as surveys, occurrence data are also implicitly contained in many other historical documents, where they are embedded in diverse linguistic structures.

Here, prerequisites for scalable information extraction of biodiversity-relevant data from written sources were investigated using content from the scientific journals published by the Museum für Naturkunde Berlin: the Deutsche Entomologische Zeitschrift and Zoosystematics and Evolution and their predecessor periodicals accessible through the Biodiversity Heritage Library.

Focussing on information concerning the observation of biological species (occurrences), together with data on habitats and related preserved specimens, a data model was developed to align natural-language text elements with facets of occurrence instances. Based on this model, a text corpus derived from the journals was manually annotated to generate ground-truth text annotations and occurrence data. The data associated with the identified observation events were serialized as RDF (Resource Description Framework) graphs and aligned with the Darwin Core standard and the data schemas of Wikidata and the Global Biodiversity Information Facility.

We outline how the annotated corpus can be used to develop and evaluate AI-based information-extraction workflows for species occurrence data from natural-language prose. In addition, the project generated insights into the acquisition and use of copyright-protected sources for text-and data-mining approaches in contrast to open access models.

actual.identification_notes: Pre-recorded presentation (speaker present in the room but answering questions via Whova). ASR renders the name 'Christian Bühling'. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Christian Bölling presented a Museum für Naturkunde Berlin project building an annotated reference corpus of historical scientific correspondence and articles from MfN journals (Deutsche Entomologische Zeitschrift, Zoosystematics and Evolution, Fossil Record and predecessors), to evaluate whether machine learning can reliably extract occurrence data at scale. A tag set (taxon, place, date, habitat, quantity, person, material, plus org/ID) aligned to Darwin Core annotates occurrences anchored at the taxon name; the first campaign found nearly 1,600 occurrence reports in 165 articles using INCEpTION. Places were matched to Wikidata (1,215 of 1,333) and taxa to GBIF IDs (1,041 of 1,154), and data serialised in RDF. He highlighted difficulties with document retrieval, erratic publisher APIs, annotation consistency and historical place names, and suggested BHL add entity recognition for persons and places and richer journal relationship metadata.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: A Darwin Core-aligned annotated corpus from MfN journals provides a reference for evaluating automated occurrence extraction from historical texts.
content_items.why_it_matters: Legacy reports contain largely untapped occurrence data; a gold-standard corpus is needed before AI extraction can be trusted.
key_points: Historical society meeting reports (e.g. Berlin Entomological Society 1915) detail dozens of observations.
A valid occurrence requires a taxon name plus place and/or date.
Places appear in almost all instances; dates, persons, quantities and materials in about a third; habitats and specimen IDs rarely.
681 distinct place entities and 741 distinct taxa were identified.
Full-text coverage for some journals was much lower than articles published; new OCR was needed for many pre-1970 articles.
datasets: Annotated reference corpus of occurrence reports from MfN journals
methods: entity linking to Wikidata and GBIF

notable_claims.claim: Nearly 1,600 occurrence reports were identified from 165 journal articles in the first annotation campaign.
Place matching to Wikidata succeeded for 1,215 of 1,333 instances; taxon matching to GBIF for 1,041 of 1,154.

recommendations: BHL could annotate persons and geographic places linked to norm data, as for taxon names.
BHL could add metadata linking related journals such as predecessors.
limitations: Document retrieval was complicated by inconsistent bibliographic databases and erratic publisher APIs.
Annotation is demanding and occurrence language has no clear boundary.
Historical place names need expert context to map to modern units.
future_work: Extend corpus with more sources and tags.
Use the corpus to evaluate and fine-tune AI relation extraction.
examples_case_studies: Reports of the Berlin Entomological Society meetings, January-March 1915

notable_moments.description: Occurrence annotation tag set.
Entity linking results.
How BHL could support such work.

content_items.title: A closer look at steps needed to extract research-ready biodiversity data from legacy literature

programme.title: A closer look at steps needed to extract research-ready biodiversity data from legacy literature
programme.session: SYM08B BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
programme.abstract: Research-ready biodiversity data must follow established standards. However, this is not easily achieved in the case of data extracted from legacy literature. The literature is unstructured and heterogenous in format, content and style, which is why data extraction presents many challenges, some of which will be illustrated during this talk. One of the problems is synonymy, a problem which goes much further than mere taxonomic or nomenclatural synonymy. Another common phenomenon is coreference, this is, two or more expressions referring to the same object. Do we need to apply or develop computer-linguistic solutions for these problems... or can we just rely on LLMs to solve them for us? This talk will discuss approaches applied in the BIOfid text mining and annotation pipeline which is under development with a focus on a German-language corpus of biodiversity legacy literature, but we expect that this approach will also help solve problems with corpora in other languages.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Gavin Kasparek'; mentions involvement in the BioFID project (ASR 'BioFit'). Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Gerwin Kasperek surveyed the obstacles to extracting research-ready data from legacy literature, using a 1969 German botanical article as an example. OCR errors propagate through NLP stages, and OCR quality evaluation itself is hard; synonyms are numerous (The Plant List had 44% synonyms and 33% accepted names) and abbreviated genus names are ambiguous across groups; taxon concepts shift over time (e.g. Linnaeus' Quercus robur) and modifiers like sensu lato/stricto matter; homonyms span taxa and places (Liparis, Paris); coreferences (C. viride, 'var. nanum') span sentences; and documents mix languages including Latin. He called for coordinated technical solutions (better OCR and its evaluation, domain-aware NLP, nomenclatural ontologies, per-sentence language detection) and taxonomic rigour (stronger backbones, Taxon Concept standards, temporal disambiguation).
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Legacy literature data can only be unlocked by combining better OCR/NLP with taxonomic rigour that accounts for synonymy, shifting concepts, coreference and mixed languages.
content_items.why_it_matters: Clarifies why AI extraction from historical texts is harder than it looks and which standards and tools are needed to get research-ready historical baselines.
key_points: Historical baselines of biodiversity need literature data.
OCR errors reduce keyword search reliability and degrade NER further.
Abbreviated names like E. rubiginosa can refer to plants, worms or fungi.
Shifting taxon concepts are more challenging than synonymy.
Coreference resolution needs general transformer NLP plus nomenclatural ontologies.
Many NLP tools assume one language per document; Latin is low-resource.

notable_claims.claim: In The Plant List, synonyms made up 44% of names with only 33% accepted names.
Shifting taxonomic concepts are far more challenging than mere synonymy problems.

recommendations: Improve OCR tools and OCR evaluation tools.
Develop comprehensive taxonomic backbones and taxon concept standards.
Integrate nomenclatural ontologies in NLP.
Detect language per sentence or paragraph.

content_items.title: Multimodality for Knowledge Extraction from Historical Entomology Literature

programme.title: Multimodality for Knowledge Extraction from Historical Entomology Literature
programme.session: SYM08B BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
programme.abstract:
Historical entomological publications combine textual descriptions and scientific illustrations that contain complementary biodiversity knowledge. While texts describe insect taxa, host plants, and ecological interactions, illustrations capture life cycles, morphological traits, and species interactions. Existing biodiversity knowledge extraction approaches mainly focus on text and rarely integrate visual information from historical illustrations.

We propose a multimodal knowledge graph for representing entities, traits, and ecological interactions extracted from historical entomological literature. As a case study, we analyze 50 articles and illustrations from Maria Sibylla Merian’s Der Raupen wunderbare Verwandelung, und sonderbare Blumennahrung (1679). Our workflow combines OCR, semantic annotation, image-region linking, and knowledge graph construction to align textual and visual information. The workflow includes: (i) extracting text with OCR, (ii) defining an annotation ontology for concepts and events in illustrations, (iii) annotating articles with these concepts, and (iv) linking illustration regions to corresponding text passages.

The workflow generates semantic triples from text and illustrations, e.g., {(tulip, instance_of, petal), (petal, has_color, purple), (caterpillar, has_shape, elongated)}. Beyond visual traits, extracted relations represent biologically relevant information such as insect-host plant associations and developmental stages. The resulting knowledge graph supports semantic enrichment and automated caption generation for historical biodiversity collections.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as Jana Hoffmann (ASR earlier 'Regiane Hoffmann'); co-presented with Sefika Efeoglu who explains the workflow. Content matches the abstract.

content_items.summary: Jana Hoffmann and Sefika Efeoglu of Senckenberg's new Semantic Data Systems and Knowledge Engineering group presented a prototype linking text and illustrations in historical entomological literature, using Maria Sibylla Merian's 1679 'Der Raupen wunderbare Verwandlung' (50 plates, digitised and published on Zenodo, soon in BHL). The workflow uses olmOCR for text, an ontology of concepts, detection of visual entities, relations and attributes in illustrations, annotation of text entities using those visual entities, merging into a multimodal sub-knowledge graph, and verbalisation into evidence-grounded captions, since historical plates often lack captions. Next steps are scaling to all 50 articles, provenance, and expert human-in-the-loop validation.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Aligning text and illustrations in a multimodal knowledge graph can generate evidence-grounded captions and recover knowledge lost by text-only extraction.
content_items.why_it_matters: Illustrations carry complementary morphological, life-stage and interaction evidence that text-only pipelines ignore.
key_points: Text describes organisms, host plants and feeding interactions; illustrations show morphology, developmental stages and spatial relations.
