content_items.title: Future interfaces for BHL

programme.title: Future interfaces for BHL
programme.session: SYM08B BHL at 20: A New Chapter for Biodiversity Literature and Data - Transforming BHL: Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation and Future Interfaces
programme.abstract:
As part of TDWG 2026 there is a workshop on future interfaces for the Biodiversity Heritage Library. The workshop will be a mostly "hands on" exploration of live demos, often based on a subset of BHL content.

This talk puts the workshop in context by surveying user interfaces employed by digital libraries in other fields. It explores different approaches to search, the use of maps, and navigating by terms or entities (such as people or taxa). It considers some of the new possibilities offered by AI-based approaches, such as searching for similar images, and wrapping complicated queries in easy to use natural language interfaces.

Having found what you are looking for, how do you want that item displayed? The talk considers various approaches, such as PDFs, such as custom-built viewers, or viewers based on the IIIF standard. Increasing adoption of IIIF has resulted in a flurry of new approaches to annotating content, including overlaying published maps on a shared map of the world, or using in-browser machine-learning tools to classify images.

The success (or otherwise) of the various demos will give insights into what interfaces will enable users to get the most value from BHL.

actual.identification_notes: Introduced as 'Professor Rod Page'; talk is a taster for his Thursday BHL workshop. Content matches the abstract's scope.

content_items.summary: Rod Page previewed live demos for Thursday's BHL interfaces workshop, emphasising he could not promise BHL would adopt them. He covered viewing (the decade-old non-mobile BHL viewer vs PDF, responsive and annotated viewers), full-text search failures (the exact 'Aphrophila gen. nov.' match ranked fourth), taxonomic name search false positives (Scutellum, Argentina), tracking name usage over time (e.g. sperm whale names), LLM-based OCR (e.g. Datalab) which he argued makes OCR essentially solved except for cost, geographic exploration (BioStor points for BHL Australia, polygon search, Allmaps georeferencing of historical maps), and image similarity and text-to-image search over ~200,000 BHL Australia pages. He hoped to have an MCP chatbot over a BHL RDF knowledge graph by Thursday and asked which ideas the community found useful.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Modern AI tools make new BHL interfaces feasible now (better OCR, image and map search, chatbots); the community must decide which are worth building.
content_items.why_it_matters: Discoverability is as important as access; these prototypes show concrete ways BHL could become more usable and connected.
key_points: The classic BHL interface has not changed in about 10 years and does not work on mobile.

GBIF is now available in RDF, inspiring a BHL knowledge graph.
questions: Which demos are useful for BHL, which are toys, and how could useful ones be implemented?

content_items.summary: The closing discussion began with an audience provocation: if GBIF and BHL are both in RDF, could an LLM use GBIF as a gazetteer to extract geographic information from all BHL pages, including the old BHL field journals project whose expedition notes could form rich information graphs? A second participant asked why BHL still lacks article-level indexing. Kearney explained content is uploaded at volume level; BioStor and later the Persistent Identifier Working Group added article data and DOIs (about 450,000 articles), but the paid work was paused during the Smithsonian transition, and she urged contributors to supply article metadata. Page added that articles could be found with a complete bibliography of life or by having AI read BHL for article pages, as NHM's work does. Kearney closed by noting BHL's need for fundraising and new ideas.
content_items.one_line_takeaway: Article-level discoverability and geographic extraction are key BHL gaps that AI may now make tractable, but resourcing remains the constraint.
content_items.why_it_matters: Highlights practical priorities for BHL (articles, places, field notes) and the link between discoverability and sustainability.
